title: Teachable Machine
content_html:
What You'll Do

In this project you'll train your own image classifier using Google's Teachable Machine — a free tool that lets you build a real machine learning model in your browser without writing any code. Using your webcam (or uploaded photos), you'll teach a model to tell different things apart: hand gestures, objects, or facial expressions.

By the end you'll have a working AI that recognises what it "sees" in real time — and, more importantly, you'll understand how machine learning actually works: collect data, train a model, test it, and spot bias when it gets things wrong. The big lesson: an AI is only as good as the data you train it on.

This one's a step up: it helps to already know roughly what AI is. Here you move from watching AI work to building a model yourself.

What You'll Need

  • Google Teachable Machine — teachablemachine.withgoogle.com (free, no login, runs entirely in your browser — your images don't leave your device unless you export them).
  • A device with a webcam (laptop, tablet or desktop). No webcam? You can upload photo files instead.
  • Chrome or Edge browser handles the camera permission most smoothly.
  • Good to know: because everything runs on your device, lots of images can slow an older machine down. Your model isn't saved automatically — export or download it before you close the tab.

Steps

  1. Go to teachablemachine.withgoogle.com, click "Get Started," choose "Image Project," then "Standard image model."
  2. Look at the layout: "Class" boxes on the left (your training images), a "Training" panel in the middle, and a live "Preview" on the right (where the model makes its guesses).
  3. Rename Class 1 and Class 2 to something real — e.g. "Thumbs Up" and "Thumbs Down," or "Book" and "Phone." Add a third class called "Nothing" or "Background" so the model learns what neither looks like.
  4. Click the webcam icon under a class and allow camera access when your browser asks.
  5. For each class, hold "Hold to Record" to capture 50–100 images — and keep moving: change your angle, distance, lighting and background.
  6. Click "Train Model." Don't close or switch tabs — training takes anywhere from 10 seconds to a few minutes.
  7. When it's done, test it live in the Preview panel: hold up the object or gesture and watch the confidence percentages change.
  8. Now try to trick it — use an object that overlaps two classes, or odd lighting — and work out why it gets it right or wrong.
  9. Go back to your worst class, add 20–30 more varied images, retrain, and test again to see it improve.
  10. Export your model: click "Export Model," choose "Tensorflow.js," and copy the link or download the files to keep your project.
  11. Show your model to a friend or the group: what does it classify, and one thing you discovered training it?

Examples to Try

  • Gesture classifier: "Thumbs Up," "Thumbs Down," "Open Palm" — recognised with over 90% confidence, even from different angles.
  • Object sorter: "Water Bottle," "Notebook," "Phone" on a desk — proving the model learned shape and colour, not just the background.
  • Expression detector: "Smiling," "Serious," "Surprised" — works well on the person who trained it but worse on someone else, which opens up a real conversation about bias in training data.

Tips

  • Variety is everything. If you record every image sitting perfectly still, your model breaks the moment the lighting or angle changes. Move around while you record.
  • Getting 100%? Don't trust it yet — test it somewhere different (by a window, farther away). If it suddenly fails, that's overfitting: it memorised instead of learning.
  • Keep your classes balanced. 200 images for one class and 20 for another makes the model lean toward the bigger one.
  • Close other browser tabs if training is slow on an older device.
  • No webcam? Use the "upload" option with photo files instead.

Think About It

  • What steps did the model go through between you showing it images and it making predictions?
  • Why did it behave differently when you changed the lighting, angle or background — what does that tell you about how it "sees"?
  • If a friend used your model, would it work as well for them? Why or why not?
  • What's the difference between the model memorising your exact images and actually learning the category?
  • Where in daily life might a classifier like this already be working — and what could go wrong if its training data was unfair or incomplete?

Challenge Yourself

  • Easy: Add a fourth class and retrain — does more categories make the model less accurate overall? Explain why.
  • Medium: Try to "break" your model with tricky inputs (poor light, partial objects, busy backgrounds). Write down three failure cases and a fix for each.
  • Hard: Swap model links with a partner and test theirs with your face/objects. Record how much the accuracy drops and explain why a model behaves differently for a "new" user — and how that connects to real worries about AI trained on narrow data.
